/-!
# Erdős Problem 938

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/938](https://www.erdosproblems.com/938)
-/
open Nat

namespace Erdos938

/--
Let $A=\{n_1 < n_2 < \cdots\}$ be the sequence of powerful numbers (if $p\mid n$ then $p^2\mid n$).
Are there only finitely many three-term progressions of consecutive terms $n_k,n_{k+1},n_{k+2}$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_938 : answer(sorry) ↔ {P : Finset ℕ | (P : Set ℕ).IsAPOfLength 3 ∧ ∃ k,
    P = {nth Powerful k, nth Powerful (k + 1), nth Powerful (k + 2)}}.Finite := by
  sorry

end Erdos938

reformulations.difference: The Lean statement counts unordered Finset triples from Nat.nth Powerful, whose enumeration includes 0, rather than qualifying indices in the usual sequence of positive powerful numbers.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every square is powerful, so the powerful numbers are infinite and Nat.nth Powerful is strictly increasing. Thus k ↦ {a_k, a_(k+1), a_(k+2)} is injective: its minimum determines a_k and hence k. For a < b < c, Set.IsAPOfLength {a,b,c} 3 is equivalent to a+c=2*b. Finiteness of the qualifying Finsets therefore equals finiteness of the qualifying indices. The positive-powerful enumeration is a_(k+1); removing the initial zero cannot change finiteness. Indeed, the extra triple {0,1,4} is not an AP. The scratch lemma complete_positive_sequence_reformulation proves the combined equivalence.
